content.subject: Electrical Measurements
content.hook: Can a wattmeter really spin backwards in a balanced three-phase circuit?
content.question: In a two-wattmeter method measuring balanced three-phase power, one wattmeter reads zero while the other reads positive. What is the load power factor?
content.answerLine: The load power factor is exactly zero point five.
explanation: Recall the standard two-wattmeter readings: wattmeter one equals V line I line cosine of thirty minus phi.
Wattmeter two equals V line I line cosine of thirty degrees plus the load phase angle phi.
For one wattmeter to read zero, cosine of thirty plus phi must equal zero at balanced conditions.
Setting thirty plus phi equal to ninety degrees reveals that the phase angle phi equals sixty degrees.
content.funFact: When the power factor falls below zero point five, the meter deflects backwards and needs coil reversal.
content.outro: Remember zero point five is the critical boundary. Subscribe for more electrical engineering exam prep!

script.narration: Recall the standard two-wattmeter readings: wattmeter one equals V line I line cosine of thirty minus phi.
Wattmeter two equals V line I line cosine of thirty degrees plus the load phase angle phi.
For one wattmeter to read zero, cosine of thirty plus phi must equal zero at balanced conditions.
Setting thirty plus phi equal to ninety degrees reveals that the phase angle phi equals sixty degrees.
Taking the cosine of sixty degrees yields a load power factor of exactly zero point five lagging.
Alternatively, use the tangent phi formula: root three times W one minus W two over their sum.
Substituting W two as zero simplifies the expression to root three times W one divided by W one.
This leaves tangent phi equal to root three, directly giving phi as sixty degrees and cosine phi as half.
Below zero point five, wattmeter two turns negative, requiring its current coil connections to be reversed.
